Jack-knife shrimp (Haliporoides sibogae) exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum body size, a trait commonly observed in deep-water penaeids. Investigations into population structure along the southeastern Australian continental slope indicate that females attain a substantially larger ultimate body length than males, with the largest documented females reaching 17.1 centimeters [Li = 17.1 centimeters]. Males, by contrast, rarely exceed a carapace length equivalent to a total body length of 13.0 centimeters [Li = 13.0 centimeters], a difference that likely reflects divergent selective pressures on reproductive investment and foraging ecology between the sexes. Captive rearing studies have provided additional insight into early life history, with hatchlings emerging at a remarkably small size; the estimated wet weight at birth for this species is approximately 0.000274 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000274 grams], a value consistent with the minute larval phase typical of planktonic caridean and penaeid shrimps. This minimal starting mass imposes a considerable energetic challenge during the early pelagic stages, as larvae must navigate a protracted period of growth before reaching a size refuge from predation.

The onset of reproductive capability in Haliporoides sibogae is tightly linked to somatic size rather than chronological age alone, though both metrics are informative. Field sampling of ovigerous females has established that puberty, defined here as the body length at which 50 percent of individuals are capable of reproducing, occurs at approximately 10 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10 centimeters] total length. This threshold size represents a critical developmental milestone, below which gonadal maturation is rarely observed. Under the stable, cool thermal regime typical of its deep-water habitat at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 14% [GSI = 14%]. This relatively modest index suggests that females allocate a significant but not overwhelming proportion of somatic resources to egg production, a pattern consistent with species that produce numerous small eggs over an extended breeding season rather than investing heavily in a single large clutch.

Longevity and the timing of key life history events in Haliporoides sibogae are profoundly influenced by the persistently cold temperatures of its bathyal environment. At a habitat temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days], a duration of about four years that is comparatively long for a penaeid shrimp and likely reflects the slowed metabolic and physiological processes operating at low thermal extremes. This two-year developmental lag before the onset of reproductive activity represents a significant pre-reproductive period during which individuals must accumulate sufficient somatic reserves and attain the critical body length necessary for successful spawning, a strategy that balances slow growth against the advantages of delayed reproduction in a stable but resource-limited environment.

Adult body mass data further underscore the pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this species, with implications for fecundity and population dynamics. The ultimate wet weight attained by females, based on maximum recorded individuals in survey catches, reaches 29.22 grams [Wwi = 29.22 grams], a mass that is nearly double that of the largest males, which plateau at an ultimate wet weight of 17.35 grams [Wwi = 17.35 grams]. This substantial disparity in adult mass is a primary driver of female-biased size at maturity, as larger body size in females directly correlates with increased brood volume and greater per-capita reproductive output. The sub-adult growth trajectory is characterized by a period of rapid mass gain following the post-larval settlement phase, during which individuals must efficiently convert ingested resources into somatic tissue to bridge the considerable gap between the minuscule hatchling mass of 0.000274 grams and the multigram mass required for reproductive competence.

Comparative analyses within the Solenoceridae family place Haliporoides sibogae as a moderate-sized member of the genus, with life-history traits shaped by its specific depth distribution and thermal niche. The body length at puberty of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters] aligns closely with values reported for other deep-water solenocerids, suggesting a conserved relationship between size and the onset of gonadal activity within this lineage. Females achieving the asymptotic length of 17.1 centimeters [Li = 17.1 centimeters] and accompanying mass of 29.22 grams [Wwi = 29.22 grams] are likely to be among the oldest individuals in the population, having survived the cumulative risks of predation and fishing mortality over nearly the full four-year lifespan (4 years) [am = 4 years] at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. Males, with their smaller ultimate size of 13.0 centimeters [Li = 13.0 centimeters] and mass of 17.35 grams [Wwi = 17.35 grams], may experience a slightly higher rate of turnover, trading off maximum growth for earlier maturity at a smaller size to increase the probability of reproducing before death in an environment where encounter rates with conspecifics may be low.
